precepts.text: Zacharias and Elisabeth walked in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless: human beings can keep God's laws.
precepts.point: The scripture also says we are gods but shall die like men, so we are the two anyway; for not keeping the commandments we die like men.

note.label: Untruthful Trinity Revisited & Ridiculous

precepts.why:
Christ said to men, “Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.” The trinity doctrine says no: only God can keep the commandments, so Christ cannot be fully a man, because a full man can't keep those laws, but a full man and a full God can. The insidiousness behind it is to make it impossible for man to keep God's commandments.

Luke answers that with John the Baptist's parents, Zacharias and Elisabeth: “And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless.” Both righteous. Walking in all the commandments. Blameless: that's perfect. So human beings can keep God's commandments, perfect as the Father in heaven. It can be done.

The scripture also says we are gods but shall die like men, so we are the two anyway; for not keeping the commandments we die like men.

Peel back the layers of confusion and the doctrine is all about removing the humanity of Christ, or keeping some of it and making him a god too, so that man can't keep the commandments: Christ kept the laws so we don't have to do anything. That's the whole premise behind the great swelling words. “The discourse of fools is irksome, and their sport is the wantonness of sin”: their sport is not having to keep the commandments. Where is Christmas, New Year, Halloween, carnival, Labor Day, the Fourth of July or birthdays in the Bible? Your three-in-one God has nothing to say about them.

note.label: The Decayed State of Liberal Women

precepts.why:
“A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow, because her hour is come”: giving birth you will be in sorrow and feel a lot of pain. “but as soon as she is delivered of the child, she remembereth no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world”. For joy a man is born into the world.

Write down Luke 1:13-14: that is when Elisabeth bore John the Baptist, and there was much joy in the world at his birth. The birth of a child is meant to bring joy, not depression. God made the woman “to be a joyful mother of children.”

So sisters should not be having kids and talking about being depressed, or using the liberal word from social media, overstimulated. Overwhelmed can be understood, because when a baby comes you will sometimes be overwhelmed, and that is why it is good to be a family and around each other, so the kids can go by the grandparents. But naturally a woman is not supposed to be like that after she gives birth. Much of the depression during and after pregnancy comes from what Esau gives you: the pills and the prenatal vitamins with folic acid, and food without nutrients. The white man is the devil.

The sisters training as midwives, doulas, doctors and nurses need to bring that lost knowledge back and teach it: the right food after pregnancy, the vitamins from food, the herbs, the steam baths. Postpartum is Leviticus 12, the days of her purification, when a woman was put in a separate place and nursed back to health by her family and the midwives.

precepts.text: When Boaz went in unto Ruth the Lord gave her conception; that is how conception happens, and the Lord gave it.
precepts.point: Thy cousin Elisabeth hath also conceived a son in her old age, for with God nothing shall be impossible; also means the same way, and the impossible thing is a barren old woman bearing, not a birth without a father.

note.label: The Nativity: the Bloodline, Birthright, & the Messiah

precepts.why:
Gabriel tells Mary, “thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son”. It is the same word used of her cousin: “And after those days his wife Elisabeth conceived”. What does it mean to conceive? To conceive you need seed; the man’s seed has to go in and fertilize the egg. Some might be confused, so Ruth shows how that happens.

“So Boaz took Ruth, and she was his wife: and when he went in unto her, the Lord gave her conception, and she bare a son.” When Boaz went in unto her, the Lord gave her conception. That is how it works: a husband goes in unto his wife, and the Lord gives the conception.

And when Luke 1:28 says the angel “came in unto her”, he came in and talked with her. He did not come in and have sex with her; he came in and talked to her, plain and simple. So when Luke 1:31 says Mary shall conceive, it is conception the way Ruth conceived, the Lord giving it when her husband came unto her. It could well have been the first time Joseph touched her that the Lord made her conceive.

precepts.text: If a woman have conceived seed and born a man child; a woman conceives seed through intercourse, the same seed Onan spilled on the ground.
precepts.point: Thy cousin Elisabeth hath also conceived a son in her old age, for with God nothing shall be impossible; also means the same way, and the impossible thing is a barren old woman bearing, not a birth without a father.

note.label: The Nativity: the Bloodline, Birthright, & the Messiah

precepts.why:
The law shows what conceiving is: “Speak unto the children of Israel, saying, If a woman have conceived seed, and born a man child: then she shall be unclean seven days”. She conceived what? Seed.

A woman conceives seed through intercourse. That is the same seed Onan spilled on the ground in Genesis 38, knowing the inheritance would not be his. It is the same exact thing.

So Luke 1:31, “thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son”, is a woman conceiving seed and bearing a man child. It is said to Mary in the same form of words as to Zacharias about Elisabeth: “thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John,” and “shalt call his name JESUS.” The same thing being done, the same thing being said.

precepts.text: The whole creature, Israel, was fashioned anew, a cloud shadowing the camp and a way through the Red Sea where all the people went defended with thy hand; overshadowing is guiding and defending.
precepts.point: Thy cousin Elisabeth hath also conceived a son in her old age, for with God nothing shall be impossible; also means the same way, and the impossible thing is a barren old woman bearing, not a birth without a father.

note.label: The Nativity: the Bloodline, Birthright, & the Messiah

precepts.why:
Luke 1:35 says “the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee”. What does overshadow mean? Wisdom of Solomon shows it: “For the whole creature in his proper kind was fashioned again anew, serving the peculiar commandments that were given unto them, that thy children might be kept without hurt”. The whole creature is Israel, the whole nation that came out of Egypt, made new, serving the peculiar commandments.

“As namely, a cloud shadowing the camp; and where water stood before, dry land appeared; and out of the Red sea a way without impediment; and out of the violent stream a green field: Wherethrough all the people went that were defended with thy hand, seeing thy marvellous strange wonders.”

What did the cloud shadowing the camp do for us at the Red Sea? It led us. It guided us through the Red Sea, and the people went through “defended with thy hand.” That is what overshadow means: to lead, guide and defend.

So when the angel says the power of the Highest shall overshadow Mary, it is not the spirit coming into her and making her pregnant. It is the Lord guiding and defending her, leading her to where she had to go.

precepts.text: Every sweet smelling tree shall overshadow Israel, for God shall lead Israel with joy; overshadow means to lead.
precepts.point: Thy cousin Elisabeth hath also conceived a son in her old age, for with God nothing shall be impossible; also means the same way, and the impossible thing is a barren old woman bearing, not a birth without a father.

note.label: The Nativity: the Bloodline, Birthright, & the Messiah

precepts.why:
Baruch gives another one. Overshadow does not mean that it got her impregnated. It means to guide her to where she had to go. “For God hath appointed that every high hill, and banks of long continuance, should be cast down, and valleys filled up, to make even the ground, that Israel may go safely in the glory of God”.

“Moreover even the woods and every sweetsmelling tree shall overshadow Israel by the commandment of God. For God shall lead Israel with joy in the light of his glory”. The trees shall overshadow Israel, for God shall lead Israel. To overshadow is to lead, guide or defend.

So in Luke 1:35 the Lord would lead Mary to Joseph. When it says overshadow thee, it means he will guide and lead her, like he led Zacharias home to his wife to lay with her. That is what it is talking about, not him overshadowing her into pregnancy.

precepts.text: Man's goings are of the Lord, how can a man then understand his own way; Mary could not understand her way, and the Lord guided her, as he guided every one of us here.
precepts.point: Thy cousin Elisabeth hath also conceived a son in her old age, for with God nothing shall be impossible; also means the same way, and the impossible thing is a barren old woman bearing, not a birth without a father.

note.label: The Nativity: the Bloodline, Birthright, & the Messiah

precepts.why:
This goes with overshadow: the Lord guided Mary, and she went and came together with her husband. “Man’s goings are of the Lord; how can a man then understand his own way?”

A man’s goings are of the Lord because the Lord guides us and overshadows us in everyday life. Sometimes you are walking in the street, something tells you to pick something up off the ground, and a car goes right by where you would have been. Why? The Lord was there guiding you.

“how can a man then understand his own way?” Remember, Mary did not understand. She said, “How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?” She was espoused to Joseph but had not yet come together with him. The Lord said, don’t worry, you are going to fulfil the scriptures; I am going to guide you. She could not understand her way, but the Most High had plans for her, and he guided her, the same way he guided every one of us here.

precepts.point: And yet for all that, when they be in the land of their enemies, I will not cast them away, neither will I abhor them, to destroy them utterly, and to break my covenant with them: for I am the Lord their God. But I will for their sakes remember the covenant of their ancestors, whom I brought forth out of the land of Egypt in the sight of the heathen. Who said bloodline is not important? The Bible says he will remember the covenant of your ancestors.

note.label: The Negro Community: A Wasteland of Tears

precepts.why:
Leviticus 26 says that even “when they be in the land of their enemies”, like today here in America, “I will not cast them away, neither will I abhor them, to destroy them utterly”. Then: “But I will for their sakes remember the covenant of their ancestors”. Who said bloodline ain’t important? The Bible says he will remember the covenant of your ancestors. Luke 1 is saying the same thing in the New Testament.

“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people, And hath raised up an horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David”. The horn of salvation is Christ. He is the king, out of the house of David. “As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets, which have been since the world began: That we should be saved from our enemies, and from the hand of all that hate us”. That is what Leviticus 26 is saying: in the land of their enemies he will not cast them away.

“To perform the mercy promised to our fathers”, our ancestors, “and to remember his holy covenant; The oath which he sware to our father Abraham”. That is the covenant of the ancestors in Leviticus 26:45, remembered for their sakes and brought to pass through Christ.

And what is it for? “that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear”. The God who brought our fathers out of Egypt in the sight of the heathen has not broken his covenant with us. He will deliver us out of the hand of our enemies so that we serve him without fear.

As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets: that we should be saved from our enemies, and from the hand of all that hate us. You want to know the answer? note.label: Why They Hated US: Walking in the Footsteps of the Persecuted

precepts.why:
Zephaniah says, “The Lord hath taken away thy judgments, he hath cast out thine enemy”. Luke shows how he does it: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people, And hath raised up an horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David”. That horn of salvation is Christ, the black Messiah.

“As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets, which have been since the world began: That we should be saved from our enemies, and from the hand of all that hate us”. Our people ask, what did we do to you? Why do you hate us so much? You want to know the answer? Christ is coming back to save you from the hand of all that hate you.

Why are you worried that your enemies hate you? Your enemies are not supposed to love you; they were created to hate you. The problem is you think you have no enemies. It is a good thing they hate us, and they should continue: they hate us when we are in our righteousness, not when we are in the streets. So don't worry about those that hate you. Rejoice.

“To perform the mercy promised to our fathers, and to remember his holy covenant”. The mercy promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob is that the kingdom is ours. That is why Zephaniah says, “Sing, O daughter of Zion; shout, O Israel; be glad and rejoice with all the heart”. Rejoice in the law, rejoice on the Sabbath, rejoice to be among the brothers and sisters. Our judgment is almost ended, and we have a short time here, so why are you bugging out? “The king of Israel, even the Lord, is in the midst of thee: thou shalt not see evil any more.”

precepts.text: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people: his people are the Israelites; that is possessive. As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets: that we should be saved from our enemies, and from the hand of all that hate us. To perform the mercy promised to our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to remember his holy covenant. That we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear: because in ancient Egypt we were fearful to serve our God, the same way some of you today are scared to even ask for a day off. Christ is going to return and redeem us from the hands of our enemies. That is Passover: deliverance.
precepts.point: Some of you are trying to save your enemy. Imagine back in Egypt, the Lord sends Moses to deliver the children of Israel, and the Israelites are fighting to save the Egyptians. That does not make sense, and it is what is happening today. The problem is many of our people do not even know who their enemy is: the enemy is the powers that enslaved and oppress you, and scripture says all the nations that touched Israel are going to answer for it.

note.label: The Book of the Wars of the Lord

precepts.why:
Wisdom says “of thy people was accepted both the salvation of the righteous, and destruction of the enemies.” There can be no salvation without your enemy being destroyed. Luke shows that this is what salvation always meant.

“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people”. His people: that is possessive, and his people are the Israelites. “And hath raised up an horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David; As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets, which have been since the world began: That we should be saved from our enemies, and from the hand of all that hate us”. Saved from who? Our enemies.

Who is your enemy, black man, black woman? Some are scared to say it for fear of losing their job. Yes, Satan is your enemy, but he works with his children, and his children are the Caucasian race. Not just the white man: the Arabs and all nations are going to pay for what they did to our people. Teach your kids that these people do not love you; from the mother’s womb we have been fighting with them. We live in a false illusion that everybody is equal and everybody loves everybody. Our enemies enslaved us, destroyed us, scattered us in slavery and took our land, and all nations hate us.

“To perform the mercy promised to our fathers, and to remember his holy covenant; The oath which he sware to our father Abraham”: the mercy promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the covenant he made with us. “That he would grant unto us, that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear”. That is Passover right there. Today we are in the hands of our enemies, and Christ is going to return and redeem us from them. And for that to happen, they all got to die, the same way the Lord drowned all the Egyptians in the sea.

“Might serve him without fear”, because in ancient Egypt we were fearful to serve our God. When we asked to go sacrifice, Pharaoh said we had too much idle time and gave us more work. It is the same today when you ask for a day off and are afraid you will be fired. Deliverance means serving him “In holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life.”

So salvation is not your enemies getting saved. Imagine Moses coming to deliver Israel and the Israelites fighting to save the Egyptians; that is what is happening today. Passover is the wars of the Lord: the Lord making war on Egypt, destroying them, and saving his people.

precepts.text: He hath visited and redeemed his people, to give knowledge of salvation unto his people.
precepts.point: The word was sent unto the children of Israel, and Peter told Cornelius, that word ye know. Remission of sins through Christ is given to his people.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.why:
“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people”. The Lord God of Israel visited and redeemed his people, not every people.

Read on to verse 77: “To give knowledge of salvation unto his people by the remission of their sins”. To whom? Unto his people. Remission of whose sins? Their sins.

So the word Peter brought to Cornelius was for the remission of their sins, and that includes Cornelius too. “in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him” because Cornelius was one of his people, an Israelite of the northern kingdom in West Manasseh, whom the Lord God of Israel came to visit and redeem. Acts 15 says it: “God at the first did visit the Gentiles, to take out of them a people for his name.” That visit, beginning with Cornelius, is the building again of the tabernacle of David, all twelve tribes reunited.

precepts.text: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he hath visited and redeemed his people; the God of the Bible is the God of Israel in both testaments.
precepts.point: He brought them forth out of the land of Egypt that He may dwell among them: I am the Lord their God. Israel should walk confident, special, and chosen above all nations of people, for the Most High is faithful and belongs to no one else; repent from spiritual fornication and return to the Most High.

note.label: Exodus 29: The Consecration of Aaron and His Sons

precepts.why:
Nothing changed across testaments. In Exodus the Lord says, “I will dwell among the children of Israel, and will be their God”, and in the gospel: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people”.

The God of the Bible is the God of Israel in both testaments, and that is the purpose of Christ: to redeem His people. He that brought them forth out of the land of Egypt that He may dwell among them is the same Lord God of Israel who visited and redeemed them.

precepts.text: Zacharias, a righteous priest of the course of Abia, had the burning of incense as his lot; each Levite was appointed his own service.
precepts.point: The fire that went out from the Lord was the same fire that came out from before the Lord in Leviticus 9 and consumed the burnt offering upon the altar.

note.label: Leviticus 10: Strange Fire and the Charge of the Priesthood

precepts.why:
Nadab and Abihu were also not the ones authorized to burn the incense. In the tabernacle service you had to be appointed to certain services and could not take a service upon yourself. Zacharias shows the pattern throughout the generations: “a certain priest named Zacharias, of the course of Abia”, righteous before God, “walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless.”

“And it came to pass, that while he executed the priest’s office before God in the order of his course, According to the custom of the priest’s office, his lot was to burn incense when he went into the temple of the Lord.” He executed the office in the order of his course, and his lot, his appointed job, was to burn incense. Each Levite was appointed his own service. Nadab and Abihu took up the censer that was not their lot, and offered what was not commanded.

precepts.text: On the eighth day they came to circumcise the child, and he was called John; John the Baptist was circumcised.
precepts.point: That did not change. On the eighth day they came to circumcise John the Baptist, and when eight days were accomplished for the circumcising of the child, his name was called Jesus, which was so named of the angel before he was conceived in the womb.

note.label: Leviticus 12: The Law of Purification After Childbirth

precepts.why:
The eighth day did not change. “on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child; and they called him Zacharias, after the name of his father. And his mother answered and said, Not so; but he shall be called John.”

John the Baptist was circumcised on the eighth day, exactly as Leviticus 12:3 and the covenant of Genesis 17 require. The law was still being kept in the days right before Christ.

precepts.text: Zacharias of the course of Abia was righteous, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless, and his lot was to burn incense in the temple; he served in the Kohathite charge.
precepts.point: The son of Zacharias was John the Baptist, a Levite; and John the Baptist was Elijah back on the earth again, come to do what was prophesied of him. There is no reincarnation, coming back as a bird or such; there is regeneration, and we come back over and over again.

note.label: Numbers 4: The Service of the Tabernacle Done in Order

precepts.why:
To the office of Eleazar pertained “the oil for the light, and the sweet incense, and the daily meat offering, and the anointing oil, and the oversight of all the tabernacle.” The burning of the sweet incense stayed in that priestly line. “There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judea, a certain priest named Zacharias, of the course of Abia: and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elisabeth.” Zacharias descended from the line of the Kohathites.

“And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless.” That is the New Testament precept for what it means to be righteous: walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless. Highlight that and commit it to memory.

“And it came to pass, that while he executed the priest’s office before God in the order of his course, According to the custom of the priest’s office, his lot was to burn incense when he went into the temple of the Lord.” The sweet incense of Eleazar’s office was still being burned by his line in the temple in the days of Herod.

precepts.text: John shall drink neither wine nor strong drink, filled with the Holy Ghost from the womb, going before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elias to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.
precepts.point: John was filled with the Holy Spirit before he was born, and Elizabeth did not sleep with an angel; Zacharias was her husband. The same way Christ was filled with the Holy Spirit before birth; the immaculate conception is a Catholic doctrine, not the scriptures.

note.label: Numbers 6: The Law of the Nazarite and the Blessing of Israel

precepts.why:
The Nazarite separated himself unto the Lord “from wine and strong drink”, drank no vinegar of wine nor liquor of grapes, and ate nothing made of the vine tree, from the kernels even to the husk. John the Baptist fell under that Nazarite vow. The angel told Zacharias, “thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John”, and “he shall be great in the sight of the Lord, and shall drink neither wine nor strong drink; and he shall be filled with the Holy Ghost, even from his mother’s womb.”

John was filled with the Holy Spirit before he was born. Elizabeth did not sleep with an angel; Zacharias was her husband. The same way Christ was filled with the Holy Spirit before birth; the immaculate conception is a Catholic doctrine, not the scriptures.

“And many of the children of Israel shall he turn to the Lord their God. And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just; to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.” A Nazarite from the womb, going before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elias.
